Article Title: Not an easy task to be coach of the Indian cricket team: Kyle Mills
Article Text:
India's coach Gautam Gambhir, left, chats with captain Shubman Gill. (AP Photo)

Excerpts

How do you think India under Gautam Gambhir are shaping up?

Do you think the scrutiny is fair when results go wrong?

One last dance for Virat Kohli and Rohit Sharma on New Zealand soil. Are you looking forward to seeing them in action?

India are now transitioning into the Shubman Gill era. What has been your first impression?

And the IPL continues to ensure a seamless transition...

In the last decade, New Zealand have been a consistent force across formats. What really changed from your playing days?

Has there been a massive upgrade in the infrastructure too?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Wellington: India under head coach Gautam Gambhir has undergone a massive transition in Test cricket but continues to enjoy some stability in the ODI format. The presence of senior players Virat Kohli Rohit Sharma , KL Rahul and Shreyas Iyer has kept the core intact for captain Shubman Gill as the team firms up its plans for the 2027 World Cup, with the ongoing ODI series against New Zealand.In an exclusive chat with TOI, former New Zealand bowler Kyle Mills opens up about coach Gambhir and the scrutiny his team faces, the changing scene in New Zealand cricket and the reasons for their recent domination.He's [Gambhir] always been a tough competitor on the field, without question. No jokes were going around at all because he always meant business on the field. Post-retirement, he entered politics and became a leader. A great tactician, a wonderful player, very professional across all facets of the game, and a tough taskmaster as well. He's a tough guy.I actually wouldn't think of another sporting team that faces as much scrutiny as the Indian cricket team, across all sports. Obviously, Manchester United have had their challenges in recent years and you've got these big teams around the world like the New York Yankees and the All Blacks, but the Indian cricket team certainly gets scrutinised, and Gambhir is the leader of that.So, it's not an easy task to be coach of the Indian cricket team, but he always has the bit between his teeth, and he's a tough customer.It's going to be a joy to have them here because they're two wonderful cricketers, and Rohit Sharma is always a cricketer that you actually like watching bat. I think it's a term that often gets used about Rohit, that he has more time than others, but the reality is he has the same amount of time as everyone else, but he just makes it look easy. Would have loved to see the two of them here for red-ball cricket too.I think he's a beautiful player. He's got all the strokes. He's a very charismatic guy. Sport's a funny game. You never own the shirt. You never own the cap. There are always people just passing through it. You think of Sachin Tendulkar. Go back to Gavaskar [Sunil], Kapil Dev. Then you go to the likes of Laxman, Dravid, Tendulkar. They all just travel through this team, and then there's been Virat and Rohit, and now they've had their turn and now we're into a new generation, and that's the beauty of sport.The IPL has done wonders, absolute wonders for the game in India, especially in white-ball cricket. You've got not just your star Indian players, but your second-, third-, fourth- and probably fifth-rated players being exposed to international cricketers in the IPL, so that advances their development. We don't have that here in New Zealand, so it's a real advantage for India.I think you need to point out that the New Zealand cricket teams are now very good, compared to where they used to be. You kind of look at the 80s, we had Sir Richard Hadlee and Martin Crowe, who effectively carried that team through a decade's worth of cricket. A bit of a poor period in New Zealand cricket history through the 90s. But without question, over the last 15 years, it's been a very good New Zealand cricket team, and I think they've been consistent in that as well, across formats.Our facilities here in New Zealand are so much better than they were. You couldn't even describe it. So the guys have great facilities now, great working environments. Through the contract system we have in New Zealand, it's a real pathway to being a career cricketer here in New Zealand. It's a real career choice to be a cricketer here in New Zealand now. So I think that's really added to the depth of New Zealand cricket. We've got players competing for spots.Obviously, we've had players like Kane Williamson, who has been a wonderful cricketer, and we've had Tim Southee and Trent Boult , who have all retired recently, but we've definitely got this new wave that's come through.Rachin Ravindra is a beautiful player, Tom Latham is a hardened international cricketer with a good all-round skill set, and our bowling group is really effective as well. We just need them to stay together and on the park. There's really good depth in the country now, which has kind of added to possibly why we've put some good results...
Article Summary: Former New Zealand bowler Kyle Mills opens up about coach Gautam Gambhir and the scrutiny his team faces. He also discusses the changing scene in New Zealand cricket and the reasons for their recent domination. Mills: "I wouldn't think of another sporting team that faces as much scrutiny as the Indian cricket team"

Article Title: Seven years later, India bowlers recreate New Zealand's 2019 World Cup semifinal nightmare
Article Text:
BCCI Photo

Arshdeep Singh starts with a maiden

NEW DELHI: New Zealand had a terrible start against India in the second ODI at the Hnry Stadium in Wellington on Saturday. The Indian bowlers were on target from the very first over and made life difficult for the home batters.The last time New Zealand scored seven or fewer runs at the end of the first five overs in an ODI was against India in the 2019 World Cup semifinal in Manchester. The Black Caps once again found themselves struggling against the Indian attack, with just seven runs on the board for the loss of one wicket after five overs.India captain Shubman Gill won the toss and elected to bowl first. Arshdeep Singh and Auqib Nabi made full use of the conditions and kept the New Zealand batters under pressure.Arshdeep gave India the perfect start by bowling a maiden over. Will Young found it difficult to deal with the left-arm pacer's movement and could not score a run in the first six balls.Auqib Nabi shared the new ball and struck in his first over. Tim Seifert, who faced five balls without scoring, tried to drive a full delivery but played the shot too early. He chipped the ball towards mid-on, where Anshul Kamboj took a good diving catch.Auqib picked up his maiden ODI wicket as New Zealand lost their first wicket at just two runs.Henry Nicholls joined Young at the crease but the runs continued to be hard to come by. Auqib kept troubling the left-hander with deliveries that moved back into him.Arshdeep also maintained the pressure from the other end. New Zealand managed only two runs in the third over and two more in the fourth.At the end of five overs, New Zealand were 7/1.
Article Summary: Auqib Nabi takes his first ODI wicket as New Zealand lose their first wicket at just two runs. New Zealand managed only two runs in the third over and two more in the fourth. The last time New Zealand scored seven or fewer runs at the end of the first five overs in an ODI was against India in the 2019 World Cup semifinal.

Article Title: Khushbu's Youth Olympics silver gives Siddi community a new sporting hero
Article Text:
Ex-India goalkeeper Juje Siddi (on the left) and Khushbu Darjada (right) are both Siddis, descendants of East Africans

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

PANAJI: Now based in London, former India goalkeeper Juje Siddi has not been following all that’s happening in Indian sports, but Khushbu Darjada’s silver medal at the Youth Olympics didn’t escape his attention.Darjada took silver in the women’s judo 63kg category in Senegal, the first Olympic medal won by any member of the Siddi community.“This is good news for everyone, particularly the community,” said Juje, the first from the Siddi tribe to represent the country and win gold at the SAFF Championship in 1997. “The feat will motivate so many others from the community to take to sport and win laurels.”Ever since his move to Salgaocar SC in 1994, Juje has stood out for his distinctive look and ‘African’ features. The goalkeeper belongs to the marginalised Siddi community, descendants of East Africans who were brought to India more than five centuries ago. The Siddis have lived in relative seclusion, most on the margins of poverty.“In the 90s, we had good support (from the govt) but now that’s no longer the case. There is private coaching being conducted but coaches are not serious enough. You must prioritise the interest of the community.If the govt steps in, there’s plenty to gain. Siddis are genetically built strong, have great physique and very good in sports,” said the Karwar-born Juje.In 1987, the Sports Authority of India (SAI), spearheaded by the then Union minister of sports Margaret Alva, set up a sports scheme to scout and train members of the community. The Siddi people had athletic abilities, and Juje was among those scouted as part of the Special Area Games (SAG) scheme.He was scouted as an athlete, but when he moved to Bengaluru for schooling, his goalkeeping abilities got noticed. He did well and made it to the India U-16 camp. His selection to the India U-19 team convinced him that he was on the right track.Soon, he was spotted by coach Norbert Gonsalves during a camp in Patiala for Salgaocar.“We were lucky to be part of the SAG scheme. They suddenly stopped the project,” said the goalkeeper.The goalkeeper enjoyed a memorable career with Salgaocar, winning every major trophy in Indian football, including the National Football League in 1999.After his retirement, he took to coaching. Juje had to move to the UK in 2019. Now, at 53, he wants to return and give back to the community that shaped him.
Article Summary: Khushbu Darjada took silver in the women’s judo 63kg category in Senegal. It was the first Olympic medal won by any member of the Siddi community. Former India goalkeeper Juje Siddi is the first Siddi to represent the country and win gold at the SAFF Championship in 1997.

Article Title: Robin Montgomery ends Maaya Rajeshwaran's Chennai Open run
Article Text:
Robin Montgomery

CHENNAI: The week offered wildcard Maaya Rajeshwaran Revathi a glimpse of what she could achieve on the big stage. But her promising run came to an end in the WTA 250 Chennai Open quarterfinals after she went down 3-6, 3-6 to American Robin Montgomery here on Friday.Montgomery, a former junior US Open champion, will face defending champion Janice Tjen, who fought back from a set down to beat Polina Kudermetova 5-7, 6-4, 6-2 in the day’s opening last-eight match.The left-handed Montgomery thrives on pace from her opponents and at times looked uncomfortable when Maaya denied her that luxury. A slow, floating backhand first-serve return from 17-year-old Maaya forced the American to generate her own pace, but she could only find the net.Maaya capitalised and went on to break serve, taking a 3-2 lead. Moreover, world No. 151 Montgomery is prone to unforced errors, having committed 59 in her previous match. Maaya, therefore, needed to keep the ball in play and allow the American’s inconsistency to work against her.The Indian failed to do so, as the 21-year-old reeled off the next four games to close out the set in just 38 minutes.Maaya’s first-serve percentage in the opening set was just 52%, and her second serves were not threatening enough.With Montgomery accustomed to playing at the net, she made good use of the volley when required.In the match between Tjen and Polina, the former took charge after losing the opening. Polina had negated Tjen’s preferred backhand slices in the opening set, with the Uzbek constructing the rallies pretty well.However, from there on, she began throwing away points, committing 45 unforced errors, most of which came in the second and third sets. Polina’s inconsistency proved costly.
Article Summary: Wildcard Maaya Rajeshwaran Revathi loses to American Robin Montgomery. Maaya will now face defending champion Janice Tjen in the quarterfinals. Tjen fought back from a set down to beat Polina Kudermetova 5-7 6-4 6-2.

Article Title: First-timer Jaypal Malviya earns LA28 quota in 10m air pistol
Article Text:
Jaypal Malviya

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

PUNE: On a day when all eyes on Manu Bhaker to win a medal and a quota place, Jaypal Malviya came unannounced to do the honours at the ISSF World Championships in Doha on Thursday.Madhya Pradesh’s Malviya, who was participating in his first international competition in the medals category, won silver in men’s 10m air pistol event and also booked India's first berth for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.Malviya, 31, scored 242.2 in the final, while China’s Hu Kai shot 243.9 to win gold. Czech Republic’s Jindrich Dubovy took bronze and the third quota place on offer with a score of 220.9.Malviya had entered the final after shooting 585 in the qualification round.Earlier, Manu Bhaker missed on winning a medal and a quota place after finishing fifth in women’s 10m air pistol event. Manu scored 179.9 in the final and a fourth-place finish would have secured at least a quota as there were two Chinese in the top-four and only one athlete from one country gets the quota from one match.Another Indian, Suruchi Singh, met a similar fate as she finished behind Manu with a score of 158.3. Manu had shot 583, while Suruchi had scored 580 to enter the final.In the men’s final, Malviya. the son of a farmer from MP’s Chhindwara district, got off to a modest start with lower 10s and some 9s in between till his first 12 shots. Though he maintained his ranking in the top-5, he changed gears after the 12 shots with 10.6, 10.2, 10.7 and 10.8 to climb up to second position in the 8-shooter final.In the last four rounds, where bronze and gold were decided, Malviya shot two 9.7s and a 10.7 to stay in the hunt, but Kai's 10.6, 10.7 and a 10.5 in the last three shots gave no chance to the Indian for gold.The final had three Chinese shooters, including Paris Games champion Yu Xie and Hu Kai, who had won all the gold medals in the four World Cups last year. The finalists also had Paris Games bronze medallist Paolo Monna of Italy, however, he crashed out of the final at fifth position, while Xie got eliminated at seventh position.“He was playing only in his first international match, that too at the World Championships. He shot really well despite being shaky in the beginning. I feel he controlled his mind well and executed his plan effectively,” India coach and former shooter Samaresh Jung told TOI
Article Summary: Madhya Pradesh's Jaypal Malviya wins silver in men's 10m air pistol event. He also booked India's first berth for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. Earlier, Manu Bhaker missed on winning a medal and a quota place.

Article Title: ‘Everybody can play on turf’: Dutch Olympic champion explains where India are falling behind
Article Text:
Floris Jan Bovelander

Mohali:

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Former Netherlands hockey star Floris jan Bovelander believes India’s vast talent pool can only translate into sustained global success if the country improves access to artificial turf pitches and strengthens grassroots development programmes.In Punjab for the Asian Champions Trophy, Bovelander, who has been involved in hockey development projects in India for more than a decade, said the biggest difference between hockey powers such as the Netherlands and India remained infrastructure at the grassroots level.“We have more than a thousand turf pitches in the Netherlands and all kids start on turf pitches,” Bovelander said. “The techniques and tactics of modern hockey are easier to learn when you play on turf from a young age.”While India possesses a far larger playing base, he noted that many pitches remain concentrated in stadiums and elite centres, limiting access for young players.“You have pitches, but sometimes you’re not allowed to play on them because they’re in stadiums. In the Netherlands, everybody can play on the turf pitches. That’s important for development,” said the two-time Olympic gold medallist.Bovelander, who helped establish the Naval Tata Hockey Academy in Jharkhand and remains involved in community-based programmes through the Bovelander Foundation, stressed that infrastructure alone was not enough.“There is often a lot of focus on high performance, but high-performance hockey benefits from strong grassroots programmes,” he added. “You need festivals, school competitions, youth leagues and good coaching. Elite players inspire young children, but you also need a strong base underneath.”As for the Indian men’s team, Bovelander said it had developed into one of the world’s most difficult sides to beat, citing back-to-back Olympic bronze medals as evidence of its progress. However, he admitted India had occasionally fallen short in key moments at major tournaments.“They are one of the top teams in the world. Maybe they are missing a little bit in the key moments, but they are always there,” he said. “If things go their way at one of the next major tournaments, they can win.”Bovelander also called for a healthy balance between experienced players and emerging talent, saying national teams should avoid relying on reputation alone.“Players should be in the team because of their performances, not because of their history,” he said. “Young players must keep pushing the experienced ones.”India’s 2016 Junior World Cup-winning generation had gone on to form the backbone of the senior side, he noted, but the challenge now was ensuring the next crop of youngsters was given similar opportunities.As far as his discussions with Punjab’s administration is concerned, Bovelander said he hoped to explore ways of contributing to coaching and grassroots initiatives, adding that expanding access to playing facilities would be among the issues he would raise with policymakers.
Article Summary: Former Netherlands hockey star Floris jan Bovelander believes India’s vast talent pool can only translate into sustained global success if the country improves access to artificial turf pitches. He has been involved in hockey development projects in India for more than a decade.

Article Title: Kylian Mbappe creates Champions League history, joins Lionel Messi in elite list
Article Text:
Real Madrid's Kylian Mbappe (AP Photo)

Mbappe milestone as Real Madrid stage comeback against AEK Athens

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Real Madrid forward Kylian Mbappe added another milestone to his impressive UEFA Champions League career on Wednesday, becoming the second-fastest player to register 100 goal contributions in the competition's history.The French superstar reached the landmark during Real Madrid's clash against AEK Athens, finding the net in the 78th minute to take his combined tally of goals and assists to 100. Mbappe has now recorded 74 goals and 26 assists in 102 Champions League appearances.Only Lionel Messi reached the milestone quicker, taking 101 matches to register 100 goal contributions. The Argentina great achieved the feat while representing Barcelona and Paris Saint-Germain (PSG) before moving to Major League Soccer (MLS), where he currently plays for Inter Miami.Cristiano Ronaldo remains at the top of the all-time Champions League goal contributions chart with 182, comprising 140 goals and 42 assists.The record-breaking moment came during an eventful encounter in Athens, where Real Madrid had to fight back after falling behind twice before eventually securing a 3-2 victory.AEK Athens made an early breakthrough through Aboubakary Koita, who opened the scoring in the 12th minute following an assist from Luka Jovic.Real Madrid thought they had found an equaliser when Vinicius Jr 's cross ended up in the net following a touch from Jude Bellingham. However, the goal was ruled out because the English midfielder was adjudged to be offside.Bellingham made up for the disallowed effort just three minutes later, producing an excellent backheel finish in the 32nd minute to bring Madrid back into the contest, as reported by Goal.com.Mbappe also had an opportunity to create danger when he picked out an unmarked Marc Cucurella, but the latter failed to make the most of the chance with his weaker foot.The hosts regained the advantage in the 75th minute, with Koita turning provider this time by setting up Stavro Pilo, who put AEK Athens on the verge of a memorable victory.However, Madrid responded almost immediately. Denzel Dumfries delivered a cross that Mbappe converted in the 78th minute, restoring parity while simultaneously bringing up his 100th Champions League goal contribution.With the match heading towards its conclusion, Federico Valverde stepped up with a stunning strike, finding the top corner to complete Madrid's comeback and seal a dramatic 3-2 win.The victory ensured that Mbappe's personal milestone was accompanied by another important result for Real Madrid in Europe.
Article Summary: Kylian Mbappe becomes second-fastest player to register 100 Champions League goal contributions. The French forward reached the landmark during Real Madrid's 3-2 win against AEK Athens on Wednesday. Only Lionel Messi reached the milestone quicker, taking 101 matches to do so.

Article Title: How NBA is looking to turn India into a billion-dollar basketball market
Article Text:
Left to right: Rajah Chaudhry (NBA's Head of Strategy, Asia Pacific), Sunny Malik (Country Head, NBA India), DeMarcus Cousins and Isiah Thomas. (Image: LinkedIn)

New Delhi:

FIRST NBA STORE IN INDIA TO OPEN IN 2027 THROUGH EXPANDED MERCHANDISING PARTNERSHIP WITH SUDITI.

Tissot are the official timing partner of the NBA. (Instagram)

Crowd at the BUDX NBA House in New Delhi, India. (Instagram)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

For a league that has spent decades turning basketball players into global icons and team jerseys into fashion statements, the NBA 's ambitions in India were never going to be restricted to television screens. The challenge, however, is turning that appeal into a sustainable business.India, with its young population, expanding digital audience and growing appetite for global sports and entertainment, represents a significant long-term opportunity for the league. But the NBA is conscious that building a presence in a cricket-dominated market requires more than securing a broadcaster and hoping fans tune in to watch games played thousands of kilometres and many timezones away.It is looking to create multiple entry points for consumers, with basketball, fashion, music, entertainment and retail forming parts of a larger commercial strategy.The latest step in that direction is the expansion of its merchandising partnership with Indian apparel company Suditi. Having worked together since 2018, the two have extended their association, with Suditi taking over the operation of NBAStore.in in October 2026.The expanded portfolio includes casual shirts and lifestyle footwear, alongside jerseys, T-shirts, jackets, sweatshirts, headwear and accessories.More significantly, the partnership will see the NBA open its first physical store in India in 2027. It is an important development for a league looking to take its relationship with fans beyond digital engagement and into everyday consumption.The idea is to make NBA merchandise a lifestyle proposition rather than limit it to conventional sports apparel. Its teams, players and iconic jerseys already have recognition beyond basketball-following circles. Just look at numerous LA Lakers, Chicago Bulls, Michael Jordan, Steph Curry, LeBron James knockoffs that get sold in the local markets. The opportunity lies in converting that cultural appeal into official merchandise sales.Long-term commercial partnerships are another important part of the NBA's business model. Swiss watchmaker Tissot, which has been associated with the league for a decade, is an example of how these relationships can evolve beyond brand visibility."Our partnerships are built on shared values, a common vision and a commitment to evolving together. The decade-long NBA association exemplifies this, with both brands continually innovating to enhance fan experience, most recently through a redesigned shot clock now adopted across the WNBA," Tissot CEO Sylvain Dolla told TimesofIndia.com.Dolla added that the same approach extended to the brand's associations across basketball, cycling and motorsport, where it works with Swiss Timing to develop sport-specific solutions. "Our objective is to contribute to each sport's growth through long-term collaboration and innovation," he added.But retail and partnerships are only part of the equation.The NBA has spent considerable time experimenting with how Indian audiences consume its product. Its broadcast journey has included a decade-long association with Sony, followed by partnerships with MTV and digital platforms. It also explored making 100 games available live on YouTube, while its three-year association with Prasar Bharati took basketball content to DD Sports and a wider free-to-air audience.The reasoning was straightforward: live games alone cannot drive growth in a market where matches are played at inconvenient hours for Indian viewers."You can't just focus on broadcast and say, 'please watch my game.' You have to do other things around the sport," said Rajah Chaudhry, NBA's Asia-Pacific head of strategy, during an interaction with TimesofIndia.com in June."The objective is not to get cocooned into just one way of saying that live games are the way to be. We want to try different ways because people like to consume games in different ways in the country. That's our objective," added Sunny Malik, NBA India's Country Head.For the 2026-27 season, NBA games are available live in India on Prime Video and NBA League Pass. The challenge is to ensure that audiences remain connected to the league even when they are not watching live action.That is where digital content assumes importance. The NBA's Indian social media platforms have accumulated more than eight million followers, generating over 1.8 billion impressions and 1.35 billion video views. Highlights, short-form clips, player stories and locally produced content allow the league to remain part of the conversation throughout the year.Its approach to fan engagement also extends beyond the screen.BUDX NBA House, which moved from Mumbai to New Delhi in May this year, brings basketball together with music, fashion, celebrity appearances and entertainment. The format is particularly relevant in India, where the NBA's cultural appeal can reach audiences who may not necessarily follow the sport closely.The initiative has also found relevance beyond India, with elements of the experience informing the league's approach in other Asia-Pacific markets.There is, however, a distinction between building awareness and building a business. Social media numbers and event attendance offer encouraging signs, but converting occasional engagement into regular viewership, merchandise sales and long-term commercial partnerships remains the bigger test.Cricket continues to command the country's sporting attention, sponsorship money and broadcast market. The NBA also has to contend with a time-zone disadvantage and the challenge of developing a sizeable paying audience for a sport that still occupies a relatively small space in India's domestic sporting landscape.The league's India strategy, therefore, is built around connecting several businesses rather than relying on one. Broadcast distribution creates visibility, digital content sustains engagement, live experiences build communities, while merchandise and retail offer opportunities to monetise that relationship.The pieces are gradually falling into place. The question is whether they can come together to create something bigger.For the NBA, India's opportunity is not merely about getting more people to watch basketball. It is about making the league part of their sporting, cultural and consumer lives.
Article Summary: The NBA is expanding its merchandising partnership with Indian apparel company Suditi. The partnership will see the NBA open its first physical store in India in 2027. It is an important development for a league looking to take its relationship with fans beyond digital engagement and into everyday consumption.

Article Title: ‘He got greedy’: Ex-India captain's blunt take on Arshdeep Singh after four-wicket haul
Article Text:
India bowler Arshdeep Singh celebrates with teammate Virat Kohli (AP/PTI)

Jadeja impressed with Anshul Kamboj

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Former India cricketer Ajay Jadeja has praised Arshdeep Singh's overall performance in India's five-wicket victory over New Zealand in the first ODI in Auckland, but believes the left-arm pacer could have avoided an expensive finish to his spell.India began their five-match ODI series with a comfortable win at Eden Park on Wednesday, November 4. In a rain-interrupted contest reduced to 32 overs per side, New Zealand were bowled out for 185 before India chased down the revised target of 143 in just 22.4 overs. Virat Kohli led the chase with a fluent 74, while Shubman Gill contributed 37 as the duo stitched together a 113-run partnership. India eventually crossed the finish line with five wickets to spare and 56 deliveries remaining.With the ball, Arshdeep was India's leading wicket-taker, claiming four wickets in his 10 overs. However, his figures of 4/70 were inflated by an expensive final over in which New Zealand tailender Blair Tickner struck him for three sixes, taking 23 runs off the over.Assessing the pacer's performance, Jadeja felt Arshdeep had been impressive for most of his spell but allowed the opportunity to complete a five-wicket haul to influence his bowling towards the end."I would call him slightly greedy. He himself said that as well. If you remove his last over, he had dismissed four batters before that and had given 40-odd runs. He got slightly greedy for the fifth wicket in the last over," Jadeja said on Sony Sports Network.Arshdeep had himself admitted after the match that the fifth wicket would have been his favourite, indicating that he was keen to complete a five-wicket haul. Despite missing out on the milestone, his four-wicket effort placed him in an exclusive group of Indian fast bowlers to achieve the feat in an ODI in New Zealand, alongside Javagal Srinath and Mohammed Shami.Jadeja, however, stressed that the expensive final over should not overshadow what Arshdeep brings to India's bowling combination. He pointed to the value of having a left-arm fast bowler in an attack that already features Jasprit Bumrah, adding that the competition for places would only benefit the team."It happens. It's natural, but Arshdeep Singh is showing that he can play in ODIs as well, which I believe is a very good thing when a left-arm seamer gets added to this attack with (Jasprit) Bumrah. The competition has increased a lot, which is very good for India," Jadeja elaborated.Jadeja also reserved praise for Anshul Kamboj, who delivered an economical spell of 2/22 from his 10 overs and walked away with the Player of the Match award.The former India batter acknowledged that Kamboj had faced questions over his bowling during his Test debut against England in 2025, particularly regarding his pace and tendency to bowl no-balls. However, he felt the youngster had shown considerable improvement in Auckland.Jadeja also suggested that Kamboj's workload before the England assignment could have contributed to his struggles, pointing out that fatigue can affect a bowler's execution. His performance against New Zealand, according to Jadeja, reflected better pace, consistency and accuracy."He bowled extremely well. The vision everyone had was that he didn't have pace when he played in England and was bowling a lot of no-balls. I think he had come after playing a lot of cricket then. So a guy also gets tired. It's not that easy. Then he was playing for the first time, but the consistency and the slight increase in his pace he showed today (Wednesday), if we talk about the accuracy amongst the four bowlers, it's Anshul Kamboj," Jadeja added.

Article Title: 'What more do you want him to prove?': Ravi Shastri questions selectors over Mohammed Shami's retirement
Article Text:
Mohammed Shami and Ravi Shastri (Image credit: Agencies)

'What more do you want a player to do?'

Shami announces retirement from Test cricket

Shami finishes with 229 Test wickets

Shami to continue playing white-ball cricket

Poll Vote & Share your view Will you continue to support Shami in his white-ball career? Yes, but I think it's time for new talents. No, I think he should retire completely. 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Former India head coach Ravi Shastri is disappointed that Mohammed Shami did not get another chance in India's Test team before announcing his retirement from the format. Shastri believes the senior fast bowler had done enough to prove his fitness through his performances in domestic cricket. He pointed out that Shami regularly played for Bengal and bowled long spells despite questions about his fitness.Shastri said playing in the gym and bowling in an actual match were two different things. According to him, a bowler's ability to bowl 10-12 overs in a match should be a better test of fitness.“What's the point of being fit in the gym if you can't bowl 10 or 12 overs in a match? Here, you've got a workhorse who's bowling for you. So, I'm a little disappointed that he didn't get another go,” Shastri said on Sony Sports Network ahead of the second ODI.The former India coach also questioned what more Shami needed to do to convince the selectors that he was ready to play international cricket.Shastri said Shami's regular appearances for Bengal and his bowling workload in first-class cricket were clear signs of his fitness.“I've heard all these press reports about his fitness not being good, but he was playing every game for Bengal.He was bowling 15-20 overs. What more do you want a player to do to prove his fitness? If he's in good form and has a good IPL, and one of your senior bowlers suddenly breaks down, you'll be looking for experience. But you've got a player like him there.“It's sad when someone who's played so well for the country has to go. I definitely thought he had another 30 or 40 wickets in him. He should have played in the last 12 months and perhaps should have been in the side as a Test-match bowler,” Shastri added.Shami played three Ranji Trophy matches for Bengal in the ongoing season and picked up 14 wickets. Shastri felt the experienced fast bowler could still have played an important role in India's Test attack.Shami announced his retirement from Test cricket on Friday, bringing an end to his 13-year career in the longest format. However, the 36-year-old made it clear that he would continue playing white-ball cricket.The fast bowler announced his decision through an Instagram post."I am leaving the white jersey, but never the memories connected to it. When I first wore India's Test jersey, I had only a dream — to do something for my country. After that every wicket, every struggle, every injury and every comeback taught me something," Shami said in his social media account."Test cricket is not just a format for me, it is a very special part of my life. Today I am deciding to retire from Test cricket with a heavy heart and unlimited beautiful memories," he added.In a video message from his farmhouse in Sahaspur Alinagar village in Uttar Pradesh's Amroha district, Shami looked back at his journey in the longest format."It's been a long journey of 13 years. Starting out from this village, I have worked very hard, seen many ups and downs, and finally, on this day, November 6, I received my Test cap and the red ball," he said.Shami also spoke about what the Test cap meant to him."After a lot of hard work, I earned this cap. Today, I completed 13 years in this journey. This cap and the red ball made me Mohammed Shami. There were many ups and downs along the way. I fell, but got back up for this cap and the ball," he said.Thanking those who supported him throughout his career, he added, "I thank my coaches, trainers and fans. A special thanks to the fans."Shami made his Test debut against the West Indies at Eden Gardens on November 6, 2013. He finished his career with 229 wickets in 64 Tests at an average of 27.71. His tally included six five-wicket hauls.He is India's sixth-highest wicket-taking fast bowler in Test cricket. Kapil Dev leads the list with 434 wickets, followed by Zaheer Khan and Ishant Sharma with 311 each, Javagal Srinath with 236 and Jasprit Bumrah with 234.Shami's ability to move the ball with both the new and old ball made him an important part of India's pace attack.Some of his best performances came in South Africa. He took 5/28 in the second innings of the Johannesburg Test during India's 2018 tour, helping the visitors win the match. On India's next tour of South Africa, he picked up eight wickets in the first Test at Centurion.His last Test appearance came in the 2023 World Test Championship final against Australia at The Oval.Injuries kept Shami out of the Indian team for long periods. He has not played for India since the 2025 Champions Trophy.However, his retirement from Test cricket does not mean the end of his playing career. He said he would continue to play white-ball cricket and could also feature in four-day matches if he remained fit."I received this cap on November 6, and today is November 6. I want to bring this journey to an end today. But I will continue to play white-ball cricket, whether in domestic competitions or the IPL."If I am fit, I will continue playing four-day cricket, but this is the end of my international Test career. My journey in this format ends here," added Shami, who is named in Bengal's squad for the Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy beginning on November 14.Shami also thanked the BCCI and the Cricket Association of Bengal (CAB) for their support."I love you all and hope many more talents emerge. A big thank you to the BCCI and the Cricket Association of Bengal," he signed off.
Article Summary: Former India head coach Ravi Shastri is disappointed that Mohammed Shami did not get another chance in India's Test team. He believes the senior fast bowler had done enough to prove his fitness through his performances in domestic cricket. The 36-year-old made it clear that he would continue playing white-ball cricket.

Former South Africa fast bowler and India's bowling coach Morne Morkel has paid tribute to Mohammed Shami following the Indian pacer's decision to retire from Test cricket, recalling how the Bengal speedster helped him settle into the Indian dressing room during his early days with the team.Morkel, who became part of head coach Gautam Gambhir 's coaching staff in 2024, said Shami played an important role in helping him understand the team's culture and communication. Article Title: Best ever! From 14 medals to 114: How India achieved more with fewer athletes at the Asian Para Games
Article Text:
Image credit: TimesofIndia.com

From 14 medals to 114: India's remarkable rise

India's Asian Para Games record

Image credit: TimesofIndia.com

Smaller contingent, bigger return

Hangzhou vs Aichi-Nagoya

Image credit: TimesofIndia.com

Athletics powers India's medal surge

India's leading medal-winning sports in Asian Para Games 2026

Image credit: TimesofIndia.com

Multiple medallists underline India's depth

Paralympic progress provides the wider context

Fourth place sets a new benchmark

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

From 14 medals in 2010 to 114 in 2026, India’s remarkable rise continued in Aichi-Nagoya as a smaller contingent surpassed its previous best, achieved 30 gold medals and secured its highest-ever finish at the continental para-sport showpiece.India’s campaign at the Asian Para Games 2026 was a triumph that few would have predicted when the size of the contingent became known. With just 167 athletes travelling to Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, the prospect of repeating the 100-plus medal haul achieved at Hangzhou in 2023 appeared ambitious. The previous edition had seen India send more than 300 athletes to the competition, returning with a record 108 medals after subsequent revisions to the original tally.But the Indian contingent defied expectations, producing an even bigger return with significantly fewer athletes. India finished the fifth edition of the Asian Para Games with 114 medals — 30 gold, 35 silver and 49 bronze — to secure fourth place, both the highest medal tally and the best finish in the country's history at the event.The numbers tell a compelling story of progress. India improved its medal tally for the fifth consecutive edition, added to its gold-medal record and finished ahead of South Korea, which had threatened to challenge its position in the final standings.More than the record itself, the achievement highlighted how far India's para-sport movement has travelled in 16 years — from a modest 14-medal return at the inaugural edition in 2010 to a fourth-place finish among Asia's leading para-sport nations.India's progress at the Asian Para Games has been steady, with each edition bringing a new high in the overall medal tally.At Guangzhou in 2010, India won 14 medals — one gold, four silver and nine bronze — to finish 15th. The 2014 edition in Incheon brought a substantial improvement, with the country collecting 33 medals, including three gold, but remaining 15th in the standings.The breakthrough arrived at Jakarta in 2018. India's medal tally rose to 72, comprising 15 gold, 24 silver and 33 bronze, while its position improved to ninth.Hangzhou in 2023 marked another major leap. India crossed the 100-medal barrier for the first time, initially returning with 111 medals before the tally was revised to 108 following a doping-related disqualification and a medal reallocation. The revised haul comprised 27 gold, 32 silver and 49 bronze, with India eventually classified sixth.Aichi-Nagoya extended that upward trajectory. India added six medals to its revised Hangzhou total, increased its gold-medal count from 27 to 30 and climbed two places to fourth.The numbers at a glance: India's medal tally increased more than eightfold between 2010 and 2026. Its gold-medal count grew from one to 30, while its position improved from 15th to fourth.The rise has not been limited to the overall tally. India has improved its standing in three successive editions since 2014, moving from 15th to ninth, then sixth and now fourth. The 2026 result represents the culmination of a sustained upward trend rather than an isolated breakthrough.The most striking feature of India's latest performance was the efficiency with which its athletes converted participation into medals.India fielded 167 athletes — 111 men and 56 women — across 11 sports at Aichi-Nagoya. That was considerably fewer than the 309 athletes listed for the Hangzhou campaign in 2023, yet the team surpassed its previous best by six medals.The comparison is revealing. India sent approximately 46 per cent fewer athletes than it did to Hangzhou, but its medal tally increased by nearly six per cent. The gold-medal count rose by three, the silver tally by three, and the bronze count remained unchanged.On a simple medals-per-athlete measure, India's return increased from approximately 0.35 medals per athlete in Hangzhou to 0.68 in Aichi-Nagoya. This is an aggregate comparison, not an individual success rate, since athletes can win multiple medals and the number of events and opportunities varies across sports.Nevertheless, the figures underline the scale of the achievement. A smaller squad did not merely match the previous edition's success; it established a new benchmark for Indian para-sport.Para-athletics was the backbone of India's campaign, delivering 65 medals — 22 gold, 19 silver and 24 bronze. That represented nearly 57 per cent of the country's overall tally and made athletics the single biggest contributor to India's fourth-place finish.Para-badminton followed with 16 medals, including three gold, five silver and eight bronze. Together, athletics and badminton accounted for 81 medals, more than 70 per cent of India's total.Swimming contributed 11 medals, comprising three silver and eight bronze. Archery added six medals, including three gold and three silver, while shooting produced five, with two gold, two silver and one bronze.Athletics' contribution also illustrates how India's progress has accelerated. At Hangzhou, para-athletics produced 52 medals, including 16 gold, 17 silver and 19 bronze. In Aichi-Nagoya, the discipline's haul rose to 65, with six additional gold medals.Badminton's contribution was different. India won 21 medals in the sport at Hangzhou, including four gold, but finished with 16 in 2026. Instead, the substantial gains in athletics and the contributions from other sports helped compensate for the decline in badminton medals.That distinction matters: the record haul reflects both the strength of India's established medal-winning disciplines and the need to broaden its success across events in future editions.India's record was supported by athletes who delivered more than once during the competition. A total of 26 Indian athletes won multiple medals, while six athletes collected multiple gold medals, demonstrating the importance of individual excellence in a campaign involving 11 sports.Archer Sheetal Devi was among the standout performers, winning two gold medals and a silver. Her two golds came in the mixed compound and individual compound events, while the silver added to her three-medal haul.Athletics provided several other multiple gold medallists. Dilip Gavit, Nishad Kumar, Pranav Soorma and Simran Sharma each won two gold medals, while shooting contributed through Mona Agarwal, who also secured two golds.Four athletes finished with three medals apiece: Sheetal Devi in archery, Thulasimathi Murugesan in badminton, Ravi Budigina in swimming and Himanshu Nandal in swimming. Their performances illustrated how athletes winning across multiple events can make a significant difference to a country's final tally.The figures also invite comparison with Hangzhou, where 25 Indian athletes won multiple medals. The increase to 26 in 2026 was modest, but the overall tally improved despite a much smaller contingent. The result points to a campaign in which medal-winning performances were concentrated among a relatively small squad.India's rise at the Asian Para Games has coincided with a significant improvement at the Paralympics, strengthening the country's standing in international para-sport.At Rio 2016, India won four medals and finished 43rd. Tokyo 2020 marked a breakthrough, with 19 medals — five gold, eight silver and six bronze — lifting India to 24th. At Paris 2024, India recorded its best Paralympic haul of 29 medals, comprising seven gold, nine silver and 13 bronze, to finish 18th.The progression at the Paralympics mirrors the broader trend at the Asian Para Games: larger medal returns, more gold medals and improvements in the standings.India's able-bodied contingent had also finished fourth at the 2026 Asian Games, although its 85-medal tally was below the 106 medals achieved at Hangzhou in 2023. The para contingent's performance offered a contrasting story of growth, with its medal count rising and its position improving.China dominated Aichi-Nagoya, finishing with 435 medals, including 207 gold. Hosts Japan were second with 186 medals, while Uzbekistan finished third with 145. India placed fourth with 114, ahead of South Korea, which collected 100 medals, including 29 gold.India's final position was not guaranteed until the closing stages. South Korea remained within reach, but its final-day return of one gold and two silver left it one gold behind India. The Indian contingent held on to fourth place with 30 gold, 35 silver and 49 bronze.The gap to third-placed Uzbekistan shows that further progress will require India to expand its medal-winning strength across disciplines. Yet the immediate achievement is significant: India has moved from 15th at the first two editions to fourth, while increasing its tally at every successive Games.The challenge now is to sustain that momentum, build a deeper pool of competitive athletes and reduce dependence on a handful of disciplines.For a contingent of just 167 athletes, 114 medals represent more than a record. They mark the latest step in a 16-year transformation of Indian para-sport — one that began with 14 medals in Guangzhou and has now culminated in a historic fourth-place finish in Aichi-Nagoya.
Article Summary: India fielded 167 athletes — 111 men and 56 women — across 11 sports at Aichi- Nagoya. India finished the fifth edition of the Asian Para Games with 114 medals — 30 gold, 35 silver and 49 bronze — to secure fourth place. It is the best finish in the country's history at the event.

NEW DELHI: Suhas Yathiraj was disappointed with his bronze medal at the Asian Para Games in Nagoya. Having beaten Indonesia's Fredy Setiawan in their group match just days earlier, the Indian shuttler had hoped to reach the final and fight for gold.Suhas lost the men's singles SL4 semifinal 23-21, 8-21, 15-21. He had chances to take the opening game but failed to convert them. After bouncing back to win the second game 21-8, he lost focus at a crucial stage of the decider.“Definitely not satisfied with bronze. I think if I had played up to my full potential, I would have definitely done better. In fact, I defeated Fredy of Indonesia in the group match in Nagoya only a few days ago,” Suhas told TimesofIndia.com from Aichi-Nagoya in Japan.“In the semifinal match, the first set was very close. I lost 23-21 and I had game point, set point, but I couldn't convert that. In the second set, I won very easily. In the third set, I think after 10-all, I sort of lost focus for two to three rallies. That is where he took the game. So, it was not my best day, I would assume. I would always love to win a gold medal. So, yes, I am a little sad from that angle,” he said.The defeat also reminded him of how important it is to perform under pressure at major tournaments.“It is the most important factor to win medals at major games because you might be training well, you might actually have the fitness and the skills. But if you don't recreate that during the major games, then probably it is of not much use in terms of professional success,” Suhas said.Suhas, an IAS officer, said he had never imagined representing India in international badminton a decade ago.In November 2016, he made his debut at the Asian Championships in Beijing and won gold. Since then, he has won several medals at major international events. These include bronze at the 2018 Asian Para Games in Jakarta, silver at the Tokyo 2020 Paralympics, another silver at the Paris 2024 Paralympics, gold at the Hangzhou Asian Para Games and bronze in Nagoya.The 43-year-old has represented India at two Paralympic Games, Tokyo in 2020 and Paris in 2024, winning silver on both occasions.With the Los Angeles 2028 Paralympics approaching, the big question is whether he can go one step further and win gold.The desire is there, but Suhas is not looking too far ahead. He wants to take things one step at a time.“If you had asked me 10 years ago, I didn't even know that I would play for India. But whenever I look at the medals and the love I have got from fans and sportspersons around the world, the journey has been quite satisfying. I have had the honour of wearing the Indian jersey and winning medals for my country,” he said.“I am grateful for what God has given me. I never imagined that I would become an IAS officer one day, an Arjuna awardee or a badminton player winning medals for India. I never imagined all this. But thanks to the Almighty for all these,” Suhas, who is also an Arjuna Award recipient, said.“So if God and destiny have been kind to me, I hope they will take me to a place that I deserve. I hope I can do the best that I can in whatever I choose to,” he added.For most people, the end of a hectic working day is a time to relax, spend time with family, play with their children or watch a movie.For Suhas, it is often time to pick up his badminton racket and head to the court. His day includes early-morning gym sessions, office work, inspections, meetings, video conferences and checking files. Despite his demanding responsibilities as an IAS officer, he makes time for badminton and follows a strict fitness routine to compete at the highest level.Balancing the two careers is not easy, but his love for the sport keeps him going.“If you choose what you love, then the journey becomes painless. You enjoy that journey. That's what I do,” Suhas said.Explaining how he manages his work and training, he said: “It is challenging. My training generally starts in the night and it always involves sacrifices. Probably others would be spending time with their family members or having leisure time. My leisure time is to play badminton. In badminton, you need an extremely high level of fitness. It's challenging, hectic but at the same time I love it.”“I don't remember eating sweets in the last many months. I can't recall when I had my last sweet. So, I almost don't eat sweets or fried food and am also quite conscious about the nutrition that I take,” he said.Suhas grew up watching Malaysian badminton great Lee Chong Wei and was inspired by his movement on the court.“Yes, I have always been inspired by so many top players in the able-bodied category. Growing up, I watched the matches of Lee Chong Wei and how he used to move around the court,” he said.“Even in India, the top shuttlers perform extremely well, whether it is Lakshya Sen, HS Prannoy or Kidambi Srikanth. I know them personally and have always admired how well they are able to compete at the top,” Suhas signed off.
Article Summary: Suhas Yathiraj was disappointed with his bronze medal at the Asian Para Games in Nagoya. The Indian shuttler lost the men's singles SL4 semifinal 23- 21, 8-21, 15-21. Suhas has represented India at two Paralympic Games, Tokyo in 2020 and Paris in 2024.

NEW DELHI: India signed off from the Aichi-Nagoya 2026 Asian Para Games with their best-ever medal haul of 114 medals as the week-long continental competition concluded with a closing ceremony at the Mizuho Park Athletics Stadium in Nagoya, Japan, on Saturday.Double gold medallists Nishad Kumar and Mona Agarwal led the Indian contingent as flag-bearers at the ceremony, marking the end of a landmark campaign in which the country's para-athletes delivered historic victories, world-record performances and podium sweeps across disciplines.India finished fourth in the overall standings with 30 gold, 35 silver and 49 bronze medals, surpassing its previous best of 108 medals at the 2022 Hangzhou Games.Held in Japan for the first time, the fifth edition of the Asian Para Games brought together around 4,000 athletes and staff from 45 countries and regions. The competition featured 18 sports, with more than 20 world records reportedly set during the seven-day event.China topped the medal table with 435 medals, including 207 gold, while hosts Japan finished second with 186 medals — 64 gold, 60 silver and 62 bronze.Uzbekistan emerged as the third-ranked nation, collecting 145 medals, including 45 gold.India's fourth-place finish was particularly significant given the size of its contingent. A total of 168 para-athletes represented the country at Aichi-Nagoya, compared with 309 at the previous edition in Hangzhou.President Droupadi Murmu congratulated the Indian contingent on its record performance, saying the achievement reflected the athletes' hard work, perseverance and self-belief.In a post on X, Murmu said the unprecedented medal haul would inspire young people to dream big, work with dedication and remain positive in the face of challenges. She also extended her congratulations to the entire Indian contingent.Para athletics was India's biggest medal contributor, accounting for 65 medals — 22 gold, 19 silver and 24 bronze. Para badminton followed with 16 medals, including three gold, five silver and eight bronze.India also won 11 medals in para swimming, seven in para table tennis, six in para archery and five in para shooting. The contingent added two medals each in para judo and para powerlifting.The closing ceremony brought together athletes, officials and dignitaries to mark the conclusion of the Games. Asian Paralympic Committee president Majid Rashed declared the event closed, highlighting the growing strength of para sport across Asia and its role in building a more inclusive society.Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi also praised the athletes' determination, teamwork and sportsmanship, describing their performances as a reminder of the “profound beauty” of para sports.The Asian Para Games began in Guangzhou, China, in 2010, evolving from the Far East and South Pacific Games Federation for the Disabled. The Aichi-Nagoya edition was the fifth staging of the event, with Doha, Qatar, scheduled to host the sixth in 2030.For India, the closing ceremony marked the end of a historic campaign — one that raised the country's medal benchmark and showcased the depth and growing strength of its para-sport movement.
Article Summary: India finished fourth in the overall standings with 30 gold, 35 silver and 49 bronze medals, surpassing its previous best of 108 medals at the 2022 Hangzhou Games. A total of 168 para-athletes represented the country at Aichi-Nagoya, compared with 309 at the previous edition in Hangzhou.

NEW DELHI: India's para-athletes produced a spectacular finish to their campaign at the Asian Para Games, registering their best-ever medal haul of 114 medals, including 30 gold, after a record-breaking final-day flourish in Aichi-Nagoya on Friday.India collected nine gold medals on the day — their biggest single-day haul of the ongoing edition — with champions emerging from badminton, archery, shooting and athletics. The country's final tally of 30 gold, 35 silver and 49 bronze surpassed its previous best of 108 medals, including 27 gold, achieved at the Hangzhou Games in 2023.The achievement was particularly significant as India competed with a contingent of 168 athletes, nearly half the size of the squad that represented the country in Hangzhou.India remained fourth in the standings at the end of its campaign, although the final positions could change after a few remaining events on Saturday.Athletics remained India's biggest medal contributor, accounting for 65 medals, 12 more than at the previous edition. On Friday, however, the spotlight was shared with a superb badminton campaign and gold-winning performances in shooting and archery. Star javelin thrower Sumit Antil led an Indian 1-2-3 finish in the men's F42-44/61-64 combined event . The reigning Paralympic and world champion threw 72.46m to defend his title, while Mahendra Gurjar took silver with 59.03m and Sandip Sanjay Sargar claimed bronze with 64.48m. Gurjar finished ahead of Sargar on Raza points, which determine rankings in combined-classification events.Pranav Soorma added another gold in the men's club throw F51, defending his title with a Games-record effort of 32.87m. India also picked up silver medals through Nimisha Chakkungalparambil in the women's long jump T47 and Parmod Bijarnia in the men's 1500m T46, where he clocked 4:09.65.India's badminton contingent delivered three gold medals, led by Paris Paralympic champion Nitesh Kumar and Games debutant Naveen Sivakumar.Nitesh defeated compatriot and Tokyo Paralympic gold medallist Pramod Bhagat 21-18, 21-16 in the men's singles SL3 final. He later added a silver medal in mixed doubles SL3-SU5 alongside Thulasimathi Murugesan.Naveen, meanwhile, defeated Indonesia's Fredy Setiawan 21-9, 21-17 to win the men's singles SL4 title. The Indian pair beat China's Yang Qiuxia and Xiao Zuxian 21-16, 21-13 in the final.The 24-year-old also secured silver in women's singles SU5 after losing 18-21, 11-21 to Yang in the final, completing a three-medal haul.Shooter Mona Agarwal added another golden chapter to India's campaign, shattering the world record to win the women's 50m rifle 3 positions SH1 title with a score of 357.5 points.The 38-year-old had earlier won the women's 10m air rifle standing SH1 gold with a Games-record score of 250.0 points, edging compatriot Avani Lekhara, who took silver with 249.6.Mona's latest triumph gave her a second gold of the Games and further underlined her standing among India's leading para-shooters. Ravi Budigina also finished with three medals, comprising two silver and one bronze.With nine gold medals on Friday and a record overall haul of 114, India signed off from its Asian Para Games campaign with its most successful performance at the continental event, surpassing the benchmark set in Hangzhou three years ago.

He had won gold at the 2023 Asian Para Games with a then-world-record throw of 73.29m before improving the mark to 74.82m in May this year.Gurjar secured silver with a throw of 59.03m, while Sargar took bronze with an effort of 64.48m.Despite Sargar recording the longer distance, Gurjar finished ahead because of his superior Raza points score, which is used to determine rankings in combined events involving athletes from different classifications.The F42, F44, F62 and F64 categories are combined in certain field events, including javelin and discus throw, to create a larger and more competitive field. The classifications cover athletes with lower-limb impairments, with some competing without prostheses and others using them.Soorma continued India's gold rush by successfully defending his men's club throw F51 title with a Games-record effort of 32.87m.The Indian had won gold in the same event at the previous edition of the Asian Para Games and claimed silver at the 2024 Paris Paralympics.South Korea's Jiwon Jung took silver with a personal-best throw of 28.40m, while Dharamvir secured bronze with 27.71m to give India another double podium finish.The F51 classification is for athletes with significant movement limitations affecting the trunk, legs and hands, with varying degrees of impairment in arm movement. Competitors perform their throws from a seated position.With Antil leading a historic Indian sweep in the javelin and Soorma retaining his title, India's para-athletes delivered another memorable day in Aichi-Nagoya.
Article Summary: Sumit Antil leads India's javelin sweep at the Asian Para Games. Pranav Soorma defends his title in the men's club throw F51 event. Mahendra Gurjar and Sandip Sanjay Sargar complete all-Indian podium finish.

Who is Himanshu Nandal?

From Paris Paralympics qualification to Asian Para Games medals

NEW DELHI: Indian para-swimmer Himanshu Nandal made his mark at the Asian Para Games 2026 in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, completing a hat-trick of bronze medals with another podium finish in the men's 100m freestyle S11 event on Friday.The 22-year-old clocked 1 minute 5.90 seconds to finish third, behind Japan's Uchu Tomita, who won gold in a Games-record time of 58.22 seconds, and China's Chuanzhen Sun, who took silver in 58.70 seconds.Nandal's latest medal added to his earlier bronze finishes in the men's 400m freestyle and 100m breaststroke S11 events. He became one of India's standout performers in para swimming, matching compatriot Ravi Budigina's three-medal haul at the Games, which comprised two silver medals and a bronze.Born blind due to optic nerve failure, Nandal grew up in a sports-oriented family in Rohtak, Haryana. MUMBAI: The official announcement arrived on Friday morning, but Manolo Marquez’s departure as head coach of Mumbai City FC seemed inevitable even as one watched him storm off the pitch and down the tunnel at the Mumbai Football Arena last Sunday.The bitterness of having just seen his side let a 2-0 lead turn into a dramatic 3-2 stoppage-time defeat to Sporting Club Delhi, in their first home match of the Indian Super League season, had been too much for the Spaniard to process.And as he disappeared into the tunnel, it only served to reinforce the pre-match rumours that his first home game as Islanders boss was very likely set to be his last.“Mumbai City FC confirms that the club and Manolo Márquez have agreed to part ways for the remainder of the MG ISL 2026/27 season,” read the club’s statement on Friday.Cracks in the relationship had already begun to appear, as the two-time champions stood winless from their first three games ahead of Delhi’s visit. Still, it was not so much the results but a mounting injury list that would lead to Marquez becoming increasingly frustrated over the uncertainty of any reinforcements arriving.The former FC Goa coach has had to contend with the challenge of losing Vikram Partap Singh, Wilmar Jordán and Leandro Otormin — three key players in attack — all to long-term injuries.In light of the situation, he didn’t hold back whenever asked for his thoughts.“I’ve been in India for seven years. When I speak, it is for a reason. When I ask for players in the squad, it is because I have enough experience in this championship,” Marquez told reporters after the gut-wrenching loss to Delhi. While he would refuse to comment when asked if he would continue in his role, he seemed prepared to accept his fate.“If the club decided to substitute the coach, they can do it,” he added. That’s exactly what Mumbai have done, making it the first managerial change this ISL season.“As with every ISL club this season, we are navigating a new era for Indian football. In many ways, this marks a fresh start for the top tier of the Indian game,” said Sujay Sharma, Mumbai City’s director of football, in the club’s statement. “We brought Manolo to the club for his experience and track record in Indian football. Article Title: In 2023, Scott McTominay's company provided £1 million through an investment firm run by his fiancée's father for a Portuguese property purchase; three years later, he faces losing his entire investme
Article Text:
Soccer Football - UEFA Champions League - FC Porto v Napoli - Estadio do Dragao, Porto, Portugal - November 4, 2026 Napoli's Scott McTominay during the warm up before the match REUTERS/Rita Franca

How McTominay's investment began

Scott McTominay and Cam Reading (Image Source: Getty)

Fortress Capital Partners collapses

Why the Portuguese property is at the centre of the court battle

The wider consequences for the Reading family

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

In May 2023, Scott McTominay’s investment company put £1 million towards a property purchase in Portugal, with plans to turn a derelict site in the Algarve into a commercial development. The money was channelled through an investment firm run by his fiancée’s father. Three years later, that firm has collapsed, the property is at the centre of a legal dispute and McTominay’s company is pursuing a £2 million claim in the High Court.The transaction dates back to May 2023, when SM Fortress, a company solely owned by McTominay, entered into a £1 million ($1.3 million) facility agreement with Fortress Capital Partners (FCP). The investment firm, operated by Ashley Reading and his daughter Cameron Reading, was intended to act as an intermediary in the purchase of a property in Lagos, in Portugal's Algarve region.McTominay's plan was to acquire a derelict two-storey property and its surrounding land, clear the site and pursue a commercial development. According to the account set out in the legal dispute, SM Fortress intended for FCP to pass the money to a Portuguese company, with the property held in trust rather than treated as an asset belonging to the investment firm.The relationship between the parties was not purely commercial. Ashley Reading ran FCP with his daughter Cameron, who is McTominay's fiancée. The footballer's investment therefore involved a company operated by members of his prospective family, a connection that has become particularly significant since the firm's collapse.McTominay also had additional money invested through the arrangement. Reports put his total exposure at approximately £2.32 million ($3 million), comprising the £1 million facility and a further £1.32 million in funds from his investment company.FCP entered administration in September 2023, only months after the Portuguese property transaction. The collapse left approximately 230 creditors facing losses estimated at close to £20 million ($26.3 million).Administrators Begbies Traynor described the firm's business model as having the characteristics of a Ponzi scheme, alleging that money from incoming investors was used to meet earlier obligations and cover existing losses rather than being supported by sustainable investment returns. The firm had attracted investors with promises of substantial returns, reportedly reaching as much as 18 per cent annually.The administrators also raised concerns about money being used in connection with luxury property investments in locations including Dubai and Spain. The collapse prompted a Metropolitan Police investigation into allegations of investment fraud, with the force confirming in 2024 that it was examining the matter.McTominay was not the only high-profile investor affected. Boyzone singer Shane Lynch was also among those reported to have suffered losses, while the administrators warned creditors that recovering their money could prove difficult.The dispute intensified after FCP became insolvent and asserted a right to sell the property in Lagos, arguing that the money used to acquire it had been lent by the firm. It also obtained an order preventing SM Fortress from seeking planning permission for the proposed commercial development.SM Fortress disputes FCP's position. Its case is that the investment firm acted as an intermediary and that the property was acquired using funds provided for that specific purpose. The disagreement is consequently about more than recovering money: it concerns who has the legal rights to the Portuguese asset and whether it should form part of FCP's insolvency estate.SM Fortress has now brought a £2 million ($2.6 million) claim against FCP in the High Court. In its response, FCP argued that McTominay's company had no ownership rights over the property and was instead an unsecured creditor, entitled to pursue whatever recovery it could establish through the insolvency process."SMF has no valid claim… over and above whatever rights it may establish as an unsecured creditor," FCP's High Court response stated.If SM Fortress is treated as an unsecured creditor, its claim would be considered alongside those of other creditors rather than giving it a separate entitlement to the property. The company is also pursuing allegations that FCP acted in breach of trust, its rights and a settlement agreement.The collapse has extended beyond the dispute with McTominay's company. Cameron Reading, who was a director of FCP between April and June 2021, was ordered to hand over hundreds of thousands of pounds relating to property sales in Dubai and Spain, according to reports. Administrators have also raised concerns about the recovery of assets and the firm's obligations to creditors.For McTominay, the investment has developed into a substantial legal and financial problem while his football career has continued in Italy. The former Manchester United midfielder joined Napoli in August for £25.7 million ($33.4 million) and went on to win the Serie A title in his first season, being named the league's best player.The High Court proceedings will determine the competing claims over the Portuguese property and the money invested through FCP. For now, the £1 million transaction made in May 2023 remains at the centre of a dispute involving a collapsed investment firm, hundreds of creditors and the family of the Scotland international's fiancée.
Article Summary: Scott McTominay's investment company put £1 million towards a property purchase in Portugal in May 2023. The money was channelled through an investment firm run by his fiancée’s father. Three years later, that firm has collapsed and the property is at the centre of a legal dispute. SM Fortress has now brought a £2 million ($2.6 million) claim against FCP in the High Court.

Article Title: Why Jobe Bellingham refuses to wear family name on his England shirt after first senior call-up, unlike brother Jude
Article Text:
Jobe Bellingham will continue wearing his first name on England’s shirt, choosing a distinct identity from older brother Jude/ Image: Instagram

Why Jobe Bellingham has his first name on his shirt

What will be different about Jude and Jobe's England shirts?

Jobe Bellingham earns first senior England call-up

Jude Bellingham's dream of playing alongside his brother

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Jobe Bellingham is set to make his senior England debut after receiving his first call-up from Thomas Tuchel, but there is one detail that will distinguish his shirt from the traditional England kit. While his older brother Jude wears BELLINGHAM above the number 10, Jobe is expected to continue using his first name on the back of his shirt, a choice he made early in his career as he began establishing himself as a footballer in his own right.Jobe began wearing his first name on the back of his shirt in the summer of 2023, when he moved from Birmingham City to Sunderland in a transfer worth £3 million. The decision was suggested by a coach who had worked with him at both clubs, and Jobe has since explained that what began as a simple preference became part of his identity as a player.Speaking to Borussia Dortmund's official website in June 2025, he said:“When I signed for Sunderland, it was suggested to me by someone, a special coach I had there who I also had in Birmingham," he said."I was still young and thought it was cool to have my own name on the back. It didn’t have any deeper meaning – but it’s become something unique. It shows that I’m going my own way."Some people don’t like it – I don’t care. You can’t follow your goal and listen to everyone at the same time.I only listen to people who know what they’re talking about – not internet critics who just spout nonsense."I just try to get better every day. And my name on my shirt is part of that.”The choice also reflects a desire to build a career independently of the attention that comes with being Jude Bellingham's younger brother. Former Sunderland manager Tony Mowbray made that point in 2024, suggesting that Jobe wanted supporters to judge him on his own performances.“I think he’s trying to create his own identity,” Mowbray said. “He doesn’t want to live off the back of his brother’s name; he wants to be the footballer that he is and show people what he can do.”England's traditional shirt printing uses a player's surname, which means Jude's shirt carries BELLINGHAM above his number 10. If Jobe followed the same convention, his shirt would also display BELLINGHAM, with the squad number providing the only visible difference between the two from the back.Jobe's preference for his first name avoids that duplication. Rather than sharing the same surname printing as his older brother, he will be identified as JOBE, continuing the practice he has followed since joining Sunderland.Jude, 23, has established himself as one of England's leading players and wears the number 10 shirt. Jobe, 21, is now taking his first step into the senior national team, having impressed at Borussia Dortmund this season. His shirt choice is a small but recognisable distinction between the brothers, particularly as they move closer to the possibility of representing England together.Jobe received his first senior England call-up on Friday, November 6, after being included in Tuchel's squad for the upcoming Nations League fixtures against Croatia and Spain.
